extracted.intended_audience: graduate students applying to the NSF GRFP (Stanford affiliates; applicants writing research proposals and personal statements)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing NSF GRFP research proposals and personal statements, focusing on intellectual merit, broader impacts, framing, feasibility, and presentation. Emphasizes strategies (start early, get feedback), reframing translational work as basic science, and making reviewer-facing choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to the rubric (explicitly tie to Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly read what is being evaluated (Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts) and tie your experiences and plans to those metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the exact NSF language where helpful; explicitly split or label sections for 'Intellectual Merit' and 'Broader Impacts' in the personal statement and research proposal. Several awardees note the effectiveness of explicitly framing statements to match NSF definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on basic science (avoid overtly clinical/translational framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame the proposal around basic science questions or methodological/technical advances rather than clinical or health applications, since NSF prioritizes basic research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reframe translational projects as investigations of underlying mechanisms or engineering/technical improvements. Avoid emphasizing disease or human health impacts in the main research narrative; put translational implications, if any, in the broader impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start early and iterate (solicit feedback often)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin planning and drafting months in advance and go through many iterations; solicit feedback from multiple sources frequently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use peer mentoring programs and ask PIs, faculty, labmates, and peers for reviews. Allow at least ~1 week for readers and plan multiple drafts; starting early gives time for iterative improvement and reframing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal statement: tell a coherent story and reveal who you are
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft the personal statement as a narrative that shows who you are, what drives you, and how your experiences shaped your path to research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid a laundry-list of accomplishments. Use a unifying theme or thread that recurs through the essay. Include personal details that provide insight into your motivations and how they connect to your proposed broader impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research plan: logical progression and clear aims
rubrics_metrics.description: The research proposal should follow a logical progression with aims that are clearly motivated and designed to address the stated question(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make aims independent so that if one aim fails, the others still produce meaningful data. Ensure the plan reads like an outline for a coherent research paper and that methods and aims connect visibly to the hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility: project should be completable and realistic (3-year horizon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose work that is achievable within the typical fellowship timeframe and consistent with your current skills and what you can reasonably acquire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers expect feasibility; avoid overly ambitious, multi-thesis projects. Emphasize how your background and planned training make the project realistic in the stated timeframe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and clarity: clearly define sections and highlight key points
rubrics_metrics.description: Use clear formatting, explicit section labels (especially for Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts), and roadmapping so reviewers can quickly find and grasp essential claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight important information in the first or last sentence of paragraphs; consider bolding or italicizing key sentences so that even a quick skim leaves the main claims and criteria evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think like a reviewer (write for non-experts outside your exact subfield)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the logic simple and clear because reviewers will likely not be in your exact subfield.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid jargon-heavy passages; emphasize motivation, central question, and why the plan advances basic understanding. Use clear signposting and explanations suitable for a knowledgeable but not specialized reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples of successful applications as models
rubrics_metrics.description: Read successful prior applications to get ideas for content, emphasis, and organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studying others' proposals can help you learn how to highlight points you want to emphasize and see practical examples of framing and format that worked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize the applicant (NSF funds individuals, not just projects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate who you are as a scientist and why you are a worthwhile investment beyond the specifics of the proposed project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show qualities that make you unique, capable, and likely to be impactful; tie past achievements and experiences to your future potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader impacts should be concrete, related to the research, and actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Design broader-impact activities that are accomplished through the research, directly relate to the project, or are supported by but complementary to the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include workshops for underprivileged students, outreach presentations, or tools shared with the scientific community. Make clear how your activities will be implemented and how they will have measurable impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reframe translational work as methodological/engineering/basic-science contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: If your background or project has translational motivations, emphasize the methodological, mechanistic, or basic-science aspects that align with NSF goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position potential translational outcomes in the broader impacts section rather than as the central intellectual-merit narrative. Describe how the work informs fundamental principles or provides broadly useful tools/techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get feedback from both experts and non-experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Solicit critiques from domain experts for technical rigor and from non-experts to ensure the broader significance and clarity are communicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts help sharpen methods and feasibility; non-experts help reveal where the big-picture motivation and alignment with NSF goals may be unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain your voice; selectively incorporate feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: While broad feedback is valuable, preserve your unique voice and do not feel obligated to adopt every suggestion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use feedback to improve clarity and rigor, but make final decisions consistent with your narrative and priorities so the application remains authentic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a unifying theme in the personal statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchor the personal statement around a concise theme that you return to, which differentiates your story and ties experiences together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A theme like 'fearless' or another personal motif can make the essay memorable and coherent rather than a clichéd or generic recounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts obvious quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: Make it easy for reviewers to identify how your proposal meets the two core NSF criteria by surfacing those claims clearly and early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit sentences summarizing intellectual merit and broader impacts, potentially formatted prominently, help even skim-readers see fit to fund.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan broader impacts for your graduate training period
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame broader impacts as activities you will realistically do during your graduate program and explain how you will sustain or implement them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State specific outreach or training activities you will undertake while at graduate school and how they are feasible given your plans and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to change aims and directions based on feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Iterate on your aims; changing the direction or experiments during drafting is acceptable and often strengthens the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple revisions can reveal better experimental approaches; flexibility can lead to higher-quality, more feasible aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate you are qualified to perform the proposed research
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide evidence (past training, techniques, preliminary data, mentorship) that you can successfully execute the plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connect prior experience and skill development plans to the proposed work so reviewers see fit between candidate capability and project needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overclaiming translational outcomes; emphasize mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not foreground potential clinical/health outcomes; instead, emphasize discovery of mechanisms or foundational advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the work has downstream applications, discuss them modestly in broader impacts rather than making them central to intellectual merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage rotation projects but align their framing with NSF expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: You may base proposals on rotation lab work but must reframe the motivation and aims to emphasize basic science or generalizable methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use technical details from a translational rotation project but present the overarching question as fundamental rather than directly clinically driven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate pitfalls and propose alternative approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify likely challenges (especially with newer technologies) and describe contingency plans or alternative experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit consideration of pitfalls demonstrates maturity in experimental design and increases reviewer confidence in likely success or useful outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align personal statement and research proposal where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure synergy between personal motivations and the research plan so reviewers can see a coherent trajectory and relationship between who you are and what you propose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie experiences and commitments in the personal statement to the skills, perspectives, and broader impacts claimed in the research plan to present a unified applicant profile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use peer-mentoring programs and structured internal deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ available institutional resources (peer mentors, proposal libraries) and internal deadlines to keep writing on schedule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer mentoring provides accountability and iterative feedback; setting internal deadlines helps manage the extended drafting process effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight key information for busy reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Because reviewers read many applications, make key claims and evidence easy to spot and remember.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place critical statements at paragraph openings or closings, use clear signposting, and ensure that a quick read yields the takeaways about intellectual merit, broader impacts, and applicant suitability.
